records.name_note: scientific_name_accepted is left unresolved because admissible sources genuinely conflict on which binomial is currently accepted. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox entry is built around Phoradendron leucarpum as its primary name, listing "Previously known as: Phoradendron flavescens, Phoradendron serotinum" -- i.e. treating leucarpum as current and serotinum as a former name. UF/IFAS's Ask IFAS EENY-110/IN267 fact sheet agrees explicitly: it names "Phoradendron leucarpum (Raf.) Reveal & M.C. Johnst." with full taxonomic authority and states "In the past, oak mistletoe has been commonly known by the synonyms Phoradendron serotinum (Raf.) M.C. Johnst. and Phoradendron flavescens (Pursh) Nutt." RHS separately lists Phoradendron flavescens (not serotinum) as the synonym of Phoradendron leucarpum, consistent with that same side. Penn State Extension's "Holiday Plants and Pets" page states the opposite relationship: "Mistletoe (Phoradendron serotinum, formerly P. flavescens or P. leucarpum)" -- treating serotinum as the current name and leucarpum as a former one. No admissible source reconciles these two treatments, so scientific_name_accepted is left blank rather than picking a side; scientific_name_given (Phoradendron leucarpum, as given in the research brief) is retained as-is.
records.toxicity_detail: Toxic to pets primarily via the berries. Penn State Extension's pet-specific guidance states that if a pet gets hold of mistletoe, toxins "particularly in the white berries, could cause vomiting, diarrhea, low blood pressure, difficulty breathing, and low heart rate." NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox separately tags Phoradendron leucarpum "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses" in its structured Problems list, and Clemson HGIC notes the berries are "toxic to humans and many animals."

outdoor_sun_exposure: left null because no admissible source frames sun exposure as something a grower controls for this species -- Phoradendron leucarpum establishes wherever a bird deposits a seed on a host tree's bark, not at a site the grower selects, so none of the full_sun/part_sun/part_shade/full_shade enum values were force-fit onto it.

soil_base/soil_drainage/soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: not applicable and left null. Phoradendron leucarpum is hemiparasitic: it draws water and inorganic nutrients through a haustorium sunk into a living host tree's tissue, not from soil (Clemson HGIC: 'a modified root (haustorium) penetrates the bark of the host tree to form a connection through which water and nutrients pass from host to parasite'; NC State: description tags it 'semiparasitic on tree limbs'). No admissible source discusses potting mix, garden soil, or soil pH for this species, and forcing a garden_bed or other soil enum value would misrepresent that it is not planted in soil at all.

water_regime/water_dry_down_target/water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: left null for the same reason -- water reaches the plant through its haustorial connection to the host tree's vascular system, not through irrigation or soil-moisture management by a grower, and no admissible source describes any watering practice for it.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: left null; as a hemiparasite obtaining nutrients from its living host tree, no admissible source describes a soil- or container-fertilizing regime for this species, nor would one make horticultural sense.

is_houseplant: set false. No admissible source supports growing this species indoors or in a container long-term, and its hemiparasitic biology structurally precludes ordinary houseplant culture -- it must stay attached to and continuously draw water/nutrients from a living host tree branch rather than being potted (Clemson HGIC haustorium description; NC State 'semiparasitic on tree limbs' description).

records.name_note: RHS gives Aconitum napellus its own explicit "Name Status: Correct" determination on a page dedicated to this species, and no admissible source disputes the binomial. NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox does not publish a dedicated Aconitum napellus page; instead it profiles the whole "Aconitum" genus on one page and lists "A. napellus" as one of three cultivars/varieties covered there (alongside A. noveboracense and A. uncinatum) under a single shared set of structured horticultural Attributes. Because that page's Light, Soil, Dimensions, USDA-zone, and Poison fields are therefore genus-wide rather than napellus-specific, this record relies on Missouri Botanical Garden's and RHS's napellus-specific pages as primary support for the categorical care fields, and treats the NC State genus data only as corroboration (flagged per-field below).
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives indoor/greenhouse day or night temperature targets for this species. In this catalog those fields are used exclusively for houseplants, and Monkshood is not one (is_houseplant: false). Missouri Botanical Garden's note that the plant 'Needs cool nights below 70 degrees F. to grow well' describes outdoor summer-climate tolerance in the St. Louis area, not an indoor/greenhouse night-temperature target, so it was not mapped onto night_f_max.

chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives a damage-onset cold temperature. RHS gives only a survival-oriented Hardiness Rating ('H7: hardy in the severest European continental climates (< -20)' degrees C) and Missouri Botanical Garden/NC State give only USDA hardiness zones (MoBoT: Zone 3 to 7; NC State genus page: USDA zones 3a-7b) -- survival/zone data, not damage-onset, which per this catalog's convention should not be mapped onto chill_damage_f.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source describes a dormancy or chilling-period care instruction beyond the plant's ordinary winter dieback as a herbaceous perennial.
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity for this species.

light_fc_min / light_fc_good / direct_sun_hours_max: no admissible source gives footcandle figures or a specific sun-hour ceiling; sources give only categorical terms (NC State genus page: 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)'; RHS 'Position: Partial shade'; MoBoT 'Sun: Full sun to part shade').

soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: RHS's own structured pH field for Aconitum napellus reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' -- a broad tolerance statement spanning the whole pH spectrum, not a numeric range -- and NC State's genus-page pH field is similarly all-inclusive ('Acid (<6.0)', 'Alkaline (>8.0)', 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)'). No admissible source gives a narrower numeric target range for this species, so both fields are left null rather than manufacturing bounds from a tolerates-everything statement.

water_dry_down_target / water_check_depth_cm / water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives numeric watering-interval, check-depth, or dormancy-duration figures for this species.
fertilize_active_months / fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_strength: no admissible source addresses fertilizing Aconitum napellus.

toxic_to_pets -- genus-page corroboration caveat: NC State Extension's 'Problem for Cats' / 'Problem for Dogs' fields and its 'Poisonous if ingested. May be fatal to humans and pets' text come from a page that profiles the whole Aconitum genus (explicitly listing A. napellus as one of three cultivars covered) rather than a dedicated napellus page, so this record treats them as corroborating rather than primary evidence. The primary support for toxic_to_pets is RHS's Aconitum-napellus-specific 'Potentially harmful' field, which separately labels a 'Pets: TOXIC if eaten; avoid skin contact' clause.

NC State's genus page also carries a structured field 'Causes Contact Dermatitis: No,' which could look like it conflicts with RHS's and Missouri Botanical Garden's skin-contact warnings. It does not: 'contact dermatitis' denotes an allergic/irritant skin rash reaction, a different mechanism from the systemic aconitine absorption through skin, mucous membranes, or open cuts that RHS and MoBoT are warning about. Both can be true simultaneously, so this was not treated as a genuine cross-source conflict on the toxicity fields.

Clemson Cooperative Extension HGIC has no dedicated factsheet for Aconitum, Aconite, Monkshood, or Wolfsbane (site search for both terms returns no matching factsheet), so Clemson contributes nothing to this record. UF/IFAS (edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu) likewise returns no Aconitum/monkshood content. Penn State Extension's only relevant hit is a bare inventory line ('Aconitum - monkshood') on its New Bolton Center Poisonous Plant Teaching Garden page, with no species-specific care or toxicity detail to cite. University of Maryland Extension's only Aconitum-specific content names it as susceptible to Verticillium wilt (not a schema field here); UMD's own 'One Hundred Poisonous Plants of Maryland' bulletin (Bulletin 314) does not include Aconitum/Monkshood among its 100 entries at all. UGA Cooperative Extension (fieldreport.caes.uga.edu) lists 'Monkshood' / 'Aconitum species' only as a bare name in two perennial-list publications, with no accompanying care data to cite.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The mechanism/symptom narrative and the claim that the toxin is 'present in the bark, flowers, fruits, leaves, roots, seeds, and stems' rest solely on NC State's genus-wide Aconitum page, which the record itself already concedes is not napellus-specific (it profiles A. napellus, A. noveboracense, and A. uncinatum together). I fetched the live NC State page and confirmed the exact 'Poisonous if ingested. May be fatal to humans and pets... Poison Part: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems' text is reused verbatim across at least eight different NC State URLs (the genus page plus separate common-name-alias pages for queen-of-poisons, aconite, wolfsbane, leopard's-bane, woman's-bane, monkshood, and helmet-flower) -- proof this is templated boilerplate, not napellus-specific content. Worse, 'bark' is physically false for this plant: the record's own is_houseplant citation (RHS) calls A. napellus an 'Herbaceous Perennial,' which has no woody/bark tissue at all -- so a toxin 'present in the bark' is a copy-paste artifact from a shared toxic-plant-parts field, not a real claim about this species. Neither RHS nor Missouri Botanical Garden (the record's declared napellus-specific primary sources) mentions any of the specific symptoms (burning lips, throat numbness, vomiting, diarrhea, muscular weakness, weak pulse, respiratory paralysis, convulsions) or the plant-part list, so none of that specific content is independently corroborated by an unproblematic species-specific citation. Separately, the citation's own claim label asserts 'High poison severity,' but the quote text given in the record's citations array never contains the word 'High' anywhere -- I confirmed NC State's real page does have a distinct 'Poison Severity: High' field, but it is absent from the quote actually cited in this record, so that portion of the claim label is not traceable to its own quote as required by the audit's first check.

NC State Plant Toolbox page for Aconitum (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/aconitum/) is a GENUS page, not species-specific, so per the rules it could not have been used for size even if reachable; the fetch machine refused/errored on it (ProxyError, 0 bytes) on every attempt, so it was skipped entirely and no content from it was used.

Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder (https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=286162&isprofile=1&gen=Aconitum) redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org, one of the hosts that refuses this fetch machine; the request was blocked before any content was returned, so it was skipped and not guessed at.

'Wildlife gardens' appears only as a suggested planting-location category ('Suggested planting locations and garden types: Cottage and informal garden, Wildlife gardens, Flower borders and beds'), which is not a statement that the plant attracts pollinators, so it was not treated as support.

records.name_note: RHS's structured taxonomy field marks "Name Status: Correct" for Salix babylonica, and all four admissible sources consulted (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS, UF/IFAS) anchor on this binomial as the accepted name -- no source resolves to a different accepted name. However, two sources carry trade-identification caveats worth flagging: NC State's profile lists "Previously known as: Salix matsudana" (a distinct species, Peking/corkscrew willow, commonly confused with S. babylonica in commerce), and Missouri Botanical Garden notes that "Some experts believe that the true species no longer exists in the wild in China and that plants being sold today under the name S. babylonica are primarily hybrids or mistakenly identified similar species." These are notes about nursery-trade identity confusion, not a genuine split over the accepted binomial itself, so scientific_name_accepted is kept as Salix babylonica.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good: these are houseplant-style ambient-environment metrics; no admissible source addresses them for this outdoor landscape tree.

records.name_note: RHS's structured taxonomy field lists this taxon's "Name Status" as "Correct," and NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox independently gives structured "Genus: Ipomoea / Species: batatas / Family: Convolvulaceae" fields for the same binomial. No admissible source disputes Ipomoea batatas as the accepted name or offers a conflicting binomial; no synonym was found on any admissible source's page for this species.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox tags Ipomoea batatas "non-toxic for cats," "non-toxic for horses," and "non-toxic for dogs," and its species page carries no poison/toxicity section at all -- an explicit non-toxicity statement, not silence. Separately, Clemson Cooperative Extension notes that cut ornamental sweetpotato vine produces a milky white sap that "can be sticky and may cause dermatitis," though the same sentence adds it "is not considered to be harmful" -- this is a human skin-contact note (irritant dermatitis from handling, not ingestion), and it is kept distinct from, not blended into, the pet-toxicity finding above. No admissible source identifies any plant part (leaves, stems, or tuberous roots) as toxic; NC State's own Edibility field lists all three as edible ("Edible leaves, tuberous roots, and stems"), so there is no edible-part/toxic-part split to record for this species.
records.cool_rest_note: Missouri Botanical Garden's culture notes describe a dig-and-store dormancy routine for the tuberous roots: "In fall before first frost, dig, dry and store tubers in a dry medium (vermiculite or peat) in a cool dry corner of the basement," with sprouted sections replanted outdoors the following spring after the last frost date.
unknowns: day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max: no admissible source gives ambient day/night air-temperature ranges for this species; sources give only soil-planting temperatures (e.g. plant after soil reaches 65°F) and USDA hardiness-zone/frost information, which are different measurements than ambient day/night air temperature.

chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives a specific damage-onset temperature for the growing plant. Clemson, NC State, UMD, and Penn State all describe frost sensitivity only qualitatively ("frost will injure top growth," "susceptible to frost so it is considered an annual," "harvest before frost"), with no degree figure. RHS's H1C hardiness rating ("can be grown outside in the summer (5 - 10°C)") is a broad UK growability/protection-need band, not a stated injury threshold -- consistent with how this catalog has treated similar RHS hardiness-letter ratings elsewhere, it was not converted into a chill_damage_f number. A distinct, separate cold figure exists for harvested-root storage (Penn State: "below 50°F will result in root rot") but that describes post-harvest chilling injury to stored roots, not damage to the living/growing plant that this field is defined to capture, so it was not used either.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity requirements; all growing guidance found is for outdoor garden/field cultivation or RHS's greenhouse note, neither of which discusses a humidity target.
light_fc_min, light_fc_good: no admissible source gives foot-candle light figures for this species.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's structured Light field defines 'Full sun' as '6 or more hours' (an open-ended lower bound, not a maximum) and 'Partial Shade' as '2-6 hours' (a ceiling for the shade category only, not a species-wide maximum) -- neither literally states a maximum sun-hours figure for the species as a whole, so this was left null rather than reusing either boundary number out of context. UMD's 'prefers 8 to 10 hours per day' sentence was also not used: it is UMD's fixed generic definition of the 'Full Sun' exposure category, reused verbatim across UMD's other vegetable pages (confirmed in this catalog's prior audit of UMD's tomato/pepper/cucumber pages), not evidence of a sweet-potato-specific ceiling.

water_check_depth_cm: Clemson's 'Water should moisten soil to at least 6 inches deep' describes how deep irrigation should penetrate the soil, not a pre-watering soil-moisture check depth, so it was not mapped to this field.

water_dry_down_target, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source frames watering in terms of a dry-down target or gives a day-count watering-frequency interval; guidance is uniformly in inches of water per week (Clemson: at least 1 in/week; UGA: 1.5 in/week split into 2-3 irrigation events; Penn State: 0.5 in/week after establishment), which does not convert to a day-interval or checked-dryness target without inventing a number not stated.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength: UGA gives a field-crop nitrogen rate (90-110 lb N/acre, 25-30% preplant with the remainder split over 'two to three applications during the season') and Clemson gives a preplant-plus-one-sidedress schedule (5-10-10 fertilizer, 30 lb/1,000 sq ft preplant, then 4 lb/100 ft of row sidedress 'before the vines cover the row') -- both describe application counts and lb-based rates for field/garden fertilizing, not a numeric day interval, named calendar months, or a liquid-dilution strength (full/half/quarter), so none of these three fields could be populated without inventing a number the sources don't state.

soil_drainage: NC State's own structured Soil Drainage field for this species lists 'Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry, Occasionally Wet' -- a broader tolerance than a strict fast-draining requirement -- while Clemson, UMD, and UGA all separately emphasize well-drained sandy/loamy soil to avoid root rot and splitting. 'moderate' was chosen as the value that best reflects NC State's own multi-value field (gooddrainage plus moisture tolerance) rather than 'fast,' even though several sources' emphasis on sandy/well-drained soil would also support a 'fast' reading; flagging this as a judgment call between two defensible enum values.

is_houseplant: set true on RHS's cultivation guidance ('May be grown outdoors in warmer regions, but best grown under glass in colder areas (minimum temperature 7-10°C)'), the same pattern this catalog has treated as houseplant/protected-structure evidence elsewhere. Missouri Botanical Garden's culture note that 'container plants and/or rooted cuttings taken in late summer may be overwintered indoors in bright sunny locations' was read as corroborating rather than load-bearing on its own. RHS's 'Suggested planting locations and garden types' list (which includes 'Patio and container plants' alongside 'Conservatory and greenhouse') was deliberately NOT cited for this field, since this catalog's own prior audit found that RHS's 'Patio and container plants' tag by itself denotes outdoor container gardening, not indoor/houseplant status.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: Verified all cited source text directly (RHS page 9185 and MoBot a587 fetched and confirmed word-for-word). The load-bearing citation is RHS's cultivation prose: 'May be grown outdoors in warmer regions, but best grown under glass in colder areas (minimum temperature 7-10°C).' 'Grown under glass' means greenhouse/conservatory cultivation, not indoor windowsill houseplant use -- and RHS's own structured 'Suggested planting locations and garden types' field for this exact species (confirmed via fetch: 'Patio and container plants / Sub-tropical / Climber and wall shrubs / Conservatory and greenhouse') lists 'Conservatory and greenhouse' as the protected-structure category, not 'Houseplants' (RHS does use a distinct 'Houseplants' tag on other species' pages when applicable, and does not apply it here). The record's own unknowns note explicitly rejects this same structured tag list's 'Patio and container plants' entry as insufficient houseplant evidence per this catalog's prior-audit precedent, but then relies on the free-text 'under glass' cultivation sentence -- which describes the identical greenhouse/conservatory growing context -- as load-bearing evidence anyway. That is an inconsistent application of the record's own standard. The remaining citation (MoBot: 'Container plants and/or rooted cuttings taken in late summer may be overwintered indoors in bright sunny locations') is explicitly self-described in the record as 'corroborating rather than load-bearing,' i.e. not sufficient alone. No admissible source actually states this species is commonly grown/kept as an indoor houseplant.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Verified both cited quotes directly against the live NC State and Clemson pages -- both quotes are accurate. But the value 'moderate' is not cleanly supported by either: Clemson's quote ('They grow best in a well-drained, loamy to sandy soil') reads as evidence for fast/well-drained soil, not a distinct 'moderate' category, and NC State's own structured field ('Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry, Occasionally Wet') is a multi-value tag list the record's own unknowns note concedes is ambiguous ('several sources' emphasis on sandy/well-drained soil would also support a "fast" reading'). Since the record itself documents this as a genuine, unresolved disagreement across its own sources rather than a clean single-value read, and picked a value anyway instead of leaving the field null, this is the refutable defect described in audit rule #2 (the VALUE itself, not just one supporting citation, is in doubt).

NC State's anchor page does publish a structured Dimensions block (Height: 6 ft. 0 in. - 10 ft. 0 in.; Width: 8 ft. 0 in. - 10 ft. 0 in.) and RHS publishes Max Height 2.5-4 metres / Max Spread 0.5-1 metres -- these were deliberately NOT recorded because the plant is a climber, not because the pages lack the data.

normalizations: 2026-08-23: eleventh batch of the "blind spots" pass. Three high-priority safety gaps, all confirmed toxic_to_pets=true: American Mistletoe (completing a classic holiday-toxic-plant trio with Poinsettia and Holly already in this catalog; also this catalog's first hemiparasitic species -- it draws water/nutrients through a haustorium into a host tree's bark, not from soil, so soil_base/soil_ph/water_regime correctly landed inapplicable rather than forced), Monkshood (aconitine, often cited as among the most acutely toxic garden perennials grown), and Common Milkweed (cardiac glycosides, the same mechanism as oleander, despite being an increasingly deliberately-planted monarch host plant). Rounded out with Golden Barrel Cactus, Weeping Willow, American Sycamore, Sweet Potato, and Creeping Jenny. All 8 confirmed genuinely uncovered by grep before landing -- Platanus occidentalis had one prior hit, but it was only an incidental mention inside a River Birch citation quote in b25 (naming sycamore as another wet-tolerant exception tree), not an actual record.

Monkshood's toxic_to_pets survived intact, but its toxicity_detail was correctly stripped after the audit found the whole symptom/mechanism narrative traced to NC State's genus-wide Aconitum page, reused verbatim across at least eight different NC State URLs (the genus page plus seven common-name-alias pages) -- and caught something the boilerplate itself gave away: the shared text lists "bark" as a poisoned plant part, which is physically impossible for an herbaceous perennial with no woody tissue at all, exactly the kind of tell that exposes copy-paste content dressed up as species-specific research.

One schema bug this batch, again caught and self-corrected by the auditor itself before this landing pass ran its own check: American Mistletoe's scientific_name_accepted was written as an empty string despite genuinely being an unresolved four-source naming conflict (NC State, UF/IFAS, and RHS treat Phoradendron leucarpum as current; Penn State Extension treats P. serotinum as current) -- the auditor named the encoding defect on its own and the batch script's cleanup step correctly nulled it.
